title: How to Think About New Ideas
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton offers a two-axis framework for deciding what to do with the flood of teaching ideas from social media, books, podcasts and CPD. The axes are the likely impact on learning and how closely an idea matches what the teacher already does. Each quadrant gets its own question: for high-impact ideas already in use, can I do it more; for ones in use but underperforming, can I do it better; for low-impact ideas not in use, why not; and for exciting new ideas, what would I need to change to make this work. He recommends trying one idea at a time, with a receptive class, starting with top-right, then bottom-right, then top-left. It is a practical piece on teacher professional learning: a way to avoid both dismissing ideas reflexively and trying too many at once.
points: Two constraints, limited time and the need to change one variable at a time, mean a teacher cannot try every idea, so a filter is needed.
The framework plots likely impact against similarity to current practice, giving each quadrant a different guiding question.
For ideas already working, the instruction is to squeeze the life out of them by using them more often and with more classes.
Before dismissing a low-impact idea, ask why, which exposes hidden beliefs or practical barriers worth examining.
Try one idea at a time with a class that is open to change and for whom failure is no disaster, working through top-right, bottom-right and then top-left.
quotes: The problem with new ideas is two-fold. First, we only have a finite amount of time in and out of lessons, to try them out. Second, to determine if any change we have tried has been effective, it is sensible to only try one idea at once so we control the other variables.

Ideas you encounter that sit in the top-right of the graph are those that you believe have a significant, positive impact on your students’ learning, and which you are already implementing. There is a danger that we think no further about such ideas because we are already doing them. I think a better approach is to ask yourself a question: Can I do it more?

If I am doing this idea with one class at a certain stage of the lesson, can I do it more times in the lesson? If I am doing it with one class, can I do it with more classes? If you have found something that is working, then squeeze the life out of it!

Here we have an idea that you are currently implementing, but it is not having the effect on learning that either you hoped it would have or that the communicator of the idea suggests that it should. The question to ask here is: Can I do it better?
The temptation here - for me, anyway - is to simply dismiss the idea and move on to the next. I think a better approach is to ask: Why?

That change could come in two different places. It may require changing some aspects of the idea to make it more suited to your subject, students or teaching style. Or, it may require changing what you currently do in the classroom to make room for the new idea.

First, to repeat what I said above, I would recommend restricting yourself to trying one idea at a time. Try it with a class that you have a good relationship with, who are accepting of change, and for whom it is not a disaster if the idea does not work out.
